From Middle English negative, negatif, from Old French negatif, from Latin negātīvus (“that denies, negative”), from negāre (“to deny”); see negate.

senses.d: Not positive or neutral; bad; undesirable; unfavourable.
ex: The high exchange rate will have a negative effect on our profits.
Customers didn’t like it: feedback was mostly negative.

senses.d: Of a number: less than zero.
Less than zero degrees Celsius or Fahrenheit.
ex: I was out in negative weather today.

senses.d: Of a test result: not positive, not detected.
ex: negative detection of.

senses.d: Of electrical charge of an electron and related particles
Denying a proposition; negating a concept.
Pessimistic; not tending to see the bright side of things.
ex: I don’t like to hang around him very much because he can be so negative about his petty problems.

senses.d: Of or relating to a photographic image in which the colours of the original, and the relations of left and right, are reversed.
Metalloidal, nonmetallic; contrasted with positive or basic.
ex: The nitro group is negative.

senses.d: Often preceded by emotion, energy, feeling, or thought: to be avoided, bad, difficult, disagreeable, painful, potentially damaging, unpleasant, unwanted.
Refusal or withholding of assents; prohibition, veto
An unfavorable point or characteristic.
A right of veto.
ex: And as to the Constitutionality of laws, that point will come before the Judges in their proper official character. In this character they have a negative on the laws.
The qualified negative of the President differs widely from this absolute negative of the British sovereign; […]

senses.d: An image in which dark areas represent light ones, and the converse.
A word that indicates negation.
ex: "Why, she is one of those persons whom negatives seem invented to describe—I doubt whether she is worth one single bad quality."

senses.d: A negative quantity.
A repetition performed with a weight in which the muscle begins at maximum contraction and is slowly extended; a movement performed using only the eccentric phase of muscle movement.
The negative plate of a voltaic or electrolytic cell.
A statement that something didn’t happen or doesn’t exist.
ex: You can’t prove a negative.

senses.d: To refuse; to veto.
ex: Poppy earnestly begged to be allowed to go with Jasmine on the roof, but this the good lady negatived with horror.
And being of warm blood he had not the phlegm tacitly to negative any proposition by unresponsive inaction.

senses.d: To contradict.
To disprove.
ex: "However, the fact that they need crystals negatives that idea...we must seek a material explanation."

senses.d: To make ineffective; to neutralize; to negate.
No; nay.
ex: "Negative Marcel. No IOC. Patient has been drinking heavily, we can give him nothing for pain."

grp.label: not positive or neutral; bad; undesirable; unfavourable

The verb is inherited from Middle English neglect, neclect, derived from Latin neglēctus, perfect passive participle of neglegō (“to make light of, disregard, not to pick up”), itself from nec (“not”) + legō (“to pick up, select”). The noun is from neglēctus (“neglect”). First attested in 1460, the noun in 1588.

c. 1598; borrowed from Latin negōtiātus, perfect active participle of negōtior (“to do business, trade”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from negotium (“business”) + -or, from nec (“not”) + otium (“leisure, ease, inactivity”).

senses.d: To confer with others in order to come to terms or reach an agreement.
To arrange or settle something by mutual agreement.
ex: We negotiated the contract to everyone's satisfaction.
The client and server computers must first negotiate a network protocol to be used.

senses.d: To succeed in coping with, getting over or navigate a hazard or obstacle.
ex: We negotiated the mountain track with difficulty.
Although the car was quite rickety, he could negotiate the curves very well.

senses.d: To transfer to another person with all the rights of the original holder; to pass, as a bill.
To transact business; to carry on trade.
ex: Jews, Turks, Armenians,[…]negotiating in this famous Emporium.

senses.d: To intrigue; to scheme.
ex: Certaine it is, shee was a busie negotiating woman.
